chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Yusuf ibn al-Sukhti, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sulayman, from al-Nawfali, from his father, from Isa ibn Abdillah, who said:

Abdullah ibn al-Hasan (peace be upon him) was near death, and his creditors gathered around him and demanded their debt from him. He said: 'I do not have what I can give you, but be satisfied with whomever you choose from my paternal uncles: Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them) or Abdullah ibn Ja'far (may Allah be pleased with him).' The creditors said: 'As for Abdullah ibn Ja'far, he is wealthy but slow to pay, but Ali ibn al-Husayn is a man who has no wealth but is truthful, and he is more beloved to us.' So they sent for him and informed him of the news. He said: 'I guarantee the money until the harvest season.' He did not have a harvest season (source of income), so the people said: 'We are satisfied, and he has guaranteed it.' When the harvest season came, Allah facilitated wealth for him, and he paid it. 'Atahah Allah' means Allah facilitated for him with wealth.

key_terms.اُحْتُضِرَ: was near death / was in the throes of death

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn guarantee a debt without having immediate wealth?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the practical application of *kafalah* (guarantee) in early Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing that personal integrity (*sidq*) can serve as sufficient collateral when material wealth is absent. Imam Zayn al-Abidin’s willingness to assume the debt, despite having no immediate assets, underscores the high status of the Ahl al-Bayt in the eyes of creditors and illustrates the theological concept of *itlah* (divine facilitation) where God provides means to fulfill obligations. The incident serves as a foundational precedent for accepting guarantees based on reputation and trustworthiness rather than just liquid capital.
